title: The Way of Kings
author: Sanderson, Brandon
review:
It seems like I'm one of the few that isn't in love with this book, I enjoyed it but didn't think it was a revelation by any stretch. Interestingly, Sanderson seems to gravitate towards classic fantasy tropes in this book and mostly eschews modern fantasy trends.

I didn't think the budget in terms of page count was used in the way I usually look for in books. This is a massive book! I expect a lot to happen with a page count like this and major events to occur. The characters don't tend to change a whole lot from the beginning of the novel (or at least past the 10% mark) to at least the 85% mark and the pages mainly are involved with exploring the history of the world or flashback sequences for the characters. I'm personally not a huge fan of flashbacks / visions unless used sparingly, they were done well here and were interesting, but a large portion of the book is taken up by them.

I'm also not completely immersed in the world, it doesn't feel quite "real" to me yet. The ideas are interesting and the fauna and weather are interesting but it doesn't seem to permeate society in the way that I'd expect. I also cringe a little bit whenever someone says "Storm off!".

All that being said, I'm continuing on with Words of Radiance and hoping the world and narrative grabs me more. For what it's worth the prose is pretty strong and understated, I also got really invested in some of the characters and they're all fairly interesting even though they didn't grow as much as I'd like.

highlights.text: They were the lowest in the army, and yet they bore the weight of kings.
Where were the Shards for ordinary men? Why hadn’t the ancients, who were so wise, created anything to help them?
What would the world be like if all men lived as the book proclaimed? Someone had to start.
“You two are a pair of nails in the same doorframe. Stern, hard, and storming annoying to pull free.”
Szeth did not object. It was not his place. He was Truthless. And he did as his masters demanded.
“Wit. It was my job to be witty.” “Saying confusing things isn’t the same as being witty.”
“The purpose of a storyteller is not to tell you how to think, but to give you questions to think upon. Too often, we forget that.”

“I haven’t faith in people any longer, old friend,” Nohadon said. “Put two men together, and they will find something to argue about. Gather them into groups, and one group will find reason to oppress or attack another.
At times, it seems to me that to be human is to want that which we cannot have. For some, this is power. For me, it is peace.”
Twenty-seven men lived. He’d finally managed to save someone. For now, that was enough.
It’s as if the future is a shattering window. The further you look, the more pieces that window breaks into. The near future can be anticipated, but the distant future … I can only guess.”
